1 
 
UNITED STATES OF AMERICA 
BEFORE THE 
FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION 
 
PJM Interconnection, L.L.C. 
) 
Docket No. ER26-3515-000 
 
COMMENTS AND REQUEST FOR CLARIFICATION 
OF AMERICAN ELECTRIC POWER SERVICE CORPORATION 
 
American Electric Power Service Corporation, on behalf of its affiliates 
Appalachian Power Company, Indiana Michigan Power Company, Kentucky Power 
Company, Kingsport Power Company, Ohio Power Company, and Wheeling Power 
Company (collectively, “AEP”), submits the following comments to and request for 
clarification of PJM Interconnection, LLC’s (“PJM’s”) proposed tariff revisions to the PJM 
Open Access Transmission Tariff (“PJM Tariff”) and Reliability Assurance Agreement 
Among Load Serving Entities (“RAA”) proposed in the above-captioned docket to 
establish Interim Resource Adequacy Service (“IRAS”) effective October 12, 2026 (the 
“IRAS Proposal”).1 
I. 
EXECUTIVE SUMMARY 
AEP recognizes that PJM faces a significant tightening of its Reliability Pricing 
Model (“RPM”) capacity market in recent years and subsequent resource adequacy 
shortfalls, and supports PJM taking action to mitigate the associated reliability risks.  AEP 
seeks narrow clarifications on certain aspects of the IRAS Proposal that impose 
 
1 PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., Proposal of PJM Interconnection, L.L.C. to Establish Interim Res. Adequacy 
Serv. and A Large Load Registry to Address Sys. Reliability, Docket No. ER26-3515 (filed Aug. 13, 2026) 
(“IRAS Proposal”).  AEP filed a doc-less motion to intervene in the captioned docket on August 17, 2026.

2 
requirements on entities that utilize the Fixed Resource Requirement Alternative (“FRR”) 
to satisfy their obligations under the RAA to commit Unforced Capacity to ensure reliable 
service to FRR loads in the PJM Region.2  
Most of AEP’s affiliate load serving entities (“LSEs”) in the PJM Region use the 
FRR Alternative.  While IRAS itself does not apply to loads in FRR service areas, the 
IRAS Proposal includes a rule that restricts FRR Entities from utilizing Existing 
Generation Capacity Resources to meet the capacity obligations of New Large Load within 
FRR service areas unless the Existing Generation Capacity Resource is procured prior to a 
set date.3  The goal of this restriction is to ensure that FRR Entities cannot poach capacity 
from the RPM market during periods of capacity shortfall.4  
Consistent with that goal, AEP requests a few points of clarification to ensure that 
the IRAS Proposal does not discriminate between FRR load and RPM load in its efforts to 
mitigate reliability risk during capacity shortfall periods in the RPM market.  First, as 
described in section III.B, the IRAS Proposal allows for IRAS to be active during periods 
of RPM capacity shortfall and to go dormant during periods of sufficient capacity in RPM.5  
AEP seeks clarification that when IRAS goes dormant, the IRAS Proposal’s restrictions on 
FRR entities also go inactive.6  Second, the IRAS Proposal allows for IRAS to reactivate 
 
2 Proposed RAA, Schedule 8.1, section D.1.  These comments solely address the aspects of the IRAS 
Proposal that affect FRR Entities and should not be construed as an endorsement of any specific provision 
of the IRAS Proposal applicable to RPM load. 
3 Id. section D.1.1. 
4 PJM Transmittal Letter at 73-74. 
5 See infra section III.B. 
6 See infra section IV.A.

3 
after a dormant period when PJM is again facing an RPM capacity shortfall.7  When IRAS 
reactivates, it redefines the load that IRAS can restrict based on a new in-service date—
only Large Loads that go into service after the new in-service date will be subject to IRAS.8  
AEP seeks clarification that when IRAS reactivates, the restrictions on using Existing 
Generation Capacity Resources also reset to an updated cutoff date.9  Finally, when IRAS 
reactivates, the reactivation determination is made just a few months before the service 
becomes active again.10  For FRR Entities, the effect is an extremely short timeline to 
comply with the IRAS Proposal’s restrictions on FRR Capacity Plans.11  AEP seeks 
clarification that there will be a buffer period for FRR Entities to develop compliant FRR 
Capacity Plans upon IRAS reactivation.12  If these clarifications are not made and the IRAS 
Proposal is implemented, the proposal will be unjust, unreasonable, and unduly 
discriminatory.  Accordingly, absent the clarifications that AEP seeks, the Commission 
should condition any approval of the IRAS on fixing these issues consistent with the 
comments below.13

II. 
CORRESPONDENCE AND COMMUNICATIONS 
Correspondence regarding this filing should be sent to the following individuals, 
who should be placed on the official service list in this proceeding:14 
John C. Crespo 
Senior Legal Counsel 
American Electric Power Service 
Corporation 
1 Riverside Plaza 
Columbus, OH  43215 
(614) 716-3727 
jccrespo@aep.com  
 
William M. Keyser 
Megan McDowell 
Steptoe LLP 
1330 Connecticut Avenue, NW 
Washington, DC  20036 
202-429-8186 
wkeyser@steptoe.com 
mmcdowell@steptoe.com  
 
III. 
BACKGROUND 
A. 
AEP 
American Electric Power Company, Inc. is one of the largest investor-owned 
electric public utility holding companies in the United States.  Its electric utility companies 
provide generation, transmission, and distribution services to more than five million 
customers in Arkansas, Indiana, Kentucky, Louisiana, Michigan, Ohio, Oklahoma, 
Tennessee, Texas, Virginia, and West Virginia.  It also partially owns entities that own 
transmission facilities in states outside of its service territories. 
American Electric Power Company, Inc.’s affiliates Appalachian Power Company, 
Indiana Michigan Power Company, Kentucky Power Company, Kingsport Power 
Company, Ohio Power Company, and Wheeling Power Company are load serving entities 
(“LSEs”) in PJM.  Accordingly, American Electric Power Service Corporation is a party 
 
14 AEP respectfully requests waiver of 18 C.F.R. § 385.203(b)(3) (2026) to allow more than two individuals 
to be designated for service on the official service list in this proceeding.

5 
to PJM’s Reliability Assurance Agreement on behalf of these LSE affiliates.  Of these 
operating companies, Appalachian Power Company, Indiana Michigan Power Company, 
Kentucky Power Company, and Wheeling Power Company are FRR Entities, meaning they 
utilize the FRR Alternative under the RAA to satisfy their RAA obligations to commit 
Unforced Capacity to ensure reliable service to loads in the PJM Region.  Thus, as FRR 
Entities, these companies do not satisfy their capacity obligations through the RPM and its 
auctions.  Rather, they supply their capacity needs from owned or contracted capacity 
resources and provide FRR Capacity Plans in advance of each Delivery Year 
demonstrating that they have sufficient Unforced Capacity to serve their load obligations, 
including satisfying the applicable reserve margin requirements. 
B. 
IRAS 
IRAS is a proposed service that will allow for Large Loads15 to interconnect in PJM 
without bringing their own capacity, on the condition that “they must reduce their load or 
switch to on-site backup resources under specific, limited emergency conditions.”16  New 
Large Loads17 can avoid being subject to IRAS reductions by bringing their own new 
capacity or procuring capacity through the Reliability Backstop Procurement.   
 
15 Proposed RAA, Article 1 – Definitions (defining Large Load):   
“Large Load” shall mean end-use customer(s) load that has a cumulative peak load of 50 
megawatts or greater at a single electrical site behind one or more points of interconnection, 
where for configurations involving multiple affiliated load facilities or multiple points of 
interconnection with affiliated load facilities behind them, all affiliated load facilities 
within a one-mile radius will be considered a single electrical site as further described in 
the PJM Manuals.   
16 PJM Transmittal Letter at 39 (footnote omitted). 
17 See infra section III.C.1, reproducing proposed definition of New Large Load in the Proposed PJM Tariff.

6 
IRAS will only apply during multi-year periods where there are insufficient 
resources to reliably meet demand in real time operations, as defined in the proposed tariff 
changes.18  During those periods, IRAS will enable PJM to reduce loads in zones/areas 
where New Large Loads have not otherwise covered their capacity needs (the New Large 
Loads that can be reduced under IRAS are considered “Eligible New Large Loads”19).  The 
IRAS Proposal sets these “active” IRAS periods based on RPM auction results:  (1) IRAS 
begins as active in the coming 2027/2028 delivery year, (2) if three consecutive years pass 
where the RPM auction clears sufficient capacity to meet the capacity requirement,20 IRAS 
goes dormant, (3) then, if the RPM auction fails to clear sufficient capacity for the third 
incremental auction in advance of a delivery year,21 IRAS reactivates for the upcoming 
delivery year.  Upon reactivation, IRAS stays active until the capacity market meets 
conditions to go dormant, as set forth in proposed Attachment DD-4, section IV(b)(iii). 
The IRAS Proposal uses the proposed definition of New Large Load as the 
mechanism to deactivate and reactivate IRAS.  IRAS obligations can only apply to eligible 
New Large Load.22  New Large Load is initially defined as Large Load with an in-service 
 
18 PJM Transmittal Letter at 1, 39-40. 
19 “Eligible New Large Loads shall mean a New Large Load eligible to provide Interim Resource Adequacy 
Service in accordance with Tariff, Attachment DD-4, section V.”  Proposed PJM Tariff, Definitions 
(defining Eligible New Large Loads); see Proposed PJM Tariff, Attachment DD-4, section V(b). 
20 The IRAS Proposal details the conditions for IRAS dormancy in proposed Attachment DD-4, section 
IV(b)(iii).  
21 The IRAS Proposal details the conditions for IRAS reactivation in proposed Attachment DD-4, section 
IV(b)(iii). 
22 See infra section III.C.1, reproducing proposed definition of New Large Load in the Proposed PJM Tariff; 
see PJM Transmittal Letter at 40-41, 69 (footnotes omitted).

7 
date after June 1, 2027.23  After three consecutive years of sufficient capacity clearing the 
RPM auction,24 the relevant in-service date for the definition of New Large Load resets.  It 
becomes June 1 of the next delivery year where sufficient capacity does not clear the RPM 
auction.25  Thus, there can be a time period where there is no load that meets the definition 
of New Large Load, because the relevant in-service date for the definition of New Large 
Load is not June 1, 2027, and has not yet reset to a new date.  Under these circumstances, 
IRAS is effectively dormant because there is no defined load for the service to apply to. 
IRAS will apply to New Large Loads that satisfy their capacity requirements via the 
RPM auction process and PJM is not proposing to extend IRAS to New Large Loads 
located in FRR Service Areas.26  However, the IRAS Proposal does require that in an FRR 
Entity’s FRR Capacity Plan, any capacity planned to serve New Large Load must be owned 
or contracted by the FRR Entity prior to a specified date:  June 1, 2027.  For ease of 
reference, these comments will refer to this rule, which the IRAS Proposal proposes to 
effectuate via revisions to the RAA Schedule 8.1, section D.1.1, as the “FRR Capacity 
Rule.” 
 
23 Id. at 38-40, 72 (footnotes omitted). 
24 As detailed in proposed Attachment DD-4, section IV(b)(iii).  
25 See section III.C.1, reproducing proposed definition of New Large Load in the Proposed PJM Tariff; see 
Proposed PJM Tariff, Attachment DD-4, section IV(b)(iii). 
26 PJM Transmittal Letter at 73.

8 
C. 
AEP’s Comments Focus on Three Proposed Amendments in the IRAS 
Proposal 
AEP’s comments and request for clarification of the IRAS Proposal focus on three 
specific proposed amendments to PJM’s governing documents:  the definition of New 
Large Load to be included in the PJM Tariff, section IV(b)(iii) of the new Attachment 
DD-4 to the PJM Tariff (which is referenced by the New Large Load definition and 
regulates when that definition is dormant and active), and the revised language in the RAA, 
Schedule 8.1, section D.1.1., which forms the FRR Capacity Rule.  These proposed 
amendments are reproduced below for ease of reference: 
1. 
PJM Tariff Definitions, Definition of New Large Load 
“New Large Load” shall mean end-use customer load that is either (a) a Large 
Load that goes into service after June 1, 2027, or (b) incremental load in-
service after June 1, 2027, that increases the existing end-use customer load 
at a single electrical site that, prior to such incremental load, did not 
previously meet the definition of Large Load.  However, to the extent three 
consecutive Delivery Years meet the requirements of Tariff, Attachment DD-
4, section IV(b)(iii), then New Large Load shall mean end-use customer load 
that is either (a) a Large Load that goes into service after June 1 of the first 
Delivery Year for which the requirements of Tariff, Attachment DD-4, 
section IV(b)(iii) are not met or (b) incremental load in-service after June 1 
of the first Delivery Year for which the requirements of Tariff, Attachment 
DD-4, section IV(b)(iii) are not met that increases the existing end-use 
customer load at a single electrical site that, prior to such incremental load, 
did not previously meet the definition of Large Load. 
2. 
PJM Tariff Attachment DD-4, section IV(b)(iii) 
In the event ([the amount of Capacity Resources committed for a given 
Delivery Year (as determined after the Third Incremental Auction) equals or 
exceeds the PJM Region Reliability Requirement determined prior to the 
Third Incremental Auction] divided by the Pool-wide Accredited UCAP 
Factor), then the Office of the Interconnection does not need any Eligible 
New Large Loads to be available to provide Interim Resource Adequacy 
Service for that Delivery Year.

9 
3. 
The FRR Capacity Rule:  RAA Schedule 8.1, section D.1.1 
An FRR Entity may not include in its FRR Capacity Plan any MW quantity 
of Existing Generation Capacity Resource27 in excess of what such FRR 
Entity owned or contracted by such FRR Entity prior to June 1, 2027, to serve 
New Large Load. 
IV. 
COMMENTS 
A. 
PJM Should Clarify that FRR Requirements Are Intended to Mirror 
the RPM Requirement Such That When IRAS is Dormant, the FRR 
Capacity Rule is Also Dormant. 
The IRAS Proposal provides a mechanism for IRAS to deactivate after three 
consecutive years of sufficient capacity clearing the RPM auction, as described above in 
section III.B.  PJM should clarify that the FRR Capacity Rule likewise deactivates when 
IRAS deactivates.  Since both the IRAS deactivation mechanism and the FRR Capacity 
Rule hinge on the definition of New Large Load, it should be evident that the FRR Capacity 
Rule is inactive when IRAS is inactive.  Nonetheless, an explicit clarification will ensure 
that no future FRR load is subject to capacity restrictions above and beyond those for RPM 
load. 
 
27 See RAA, Article 1 – Definitions (defining Existing Generation Capacity Resource):   
“Existing Generation Capacity Resource” shall mean, for purposes of the must-offer 
requirement and mitigation of offers for any RPM Auction for a Delivery Year, a 
Generation Capacity Resource that, as of the date on which bidding commences for such 
auction:  (a) is in service; or (b) is not yet in service, but has cleared any RPM Auction for 
any prior Delivery Year.  A Generation Capacity Resource shall be deemed to be in service 
if interconnection service has ever commenced (for resources located in the PJM Region), 
or if it is physically and electrically interconnected to an external Control Area and is in 
full commercial operation (for resources not located in the PJM Region).  The additional 
megawatts of a Generation Capacity Resource that is being, or has been, modified to 
increase the number of megawatts of available installed capacity thereof shall not be 
deemed to be an Existing Generation Capacity Resource until such time as those megawatts 
(a) are in service; or (b) are not yet in service, but have cleared any RPM Auction for any 
prior Delivery Year.

10 
The IRAS Proposal defines New Large Load as Large Load that goes into service 
after June 1, 2027.  However, once system conditions are met such that IRAS is no longer 
necessary, IRAS is deactivated.  When this happens, the definition of New Large Load 
becomes Large Load that goes into service after June 1 of the next Delivery Year that PJM 
faces capacity scarcity and IRAS must be reactivated.28  
Under the proposed FRR Capacity Rule, “An FRR Entity may not include in its 
FRR Capacity Plan any MW quantity of Existing Generation Capacity Resource in excess 
of what such FRR Entity owned or contracted by such FRR Entity prior to June 1, 2027, 
to serve New Large Load.”  The final clause “to serve New Large Load” clearly modifies 
the entire sentence.  The inclusion of this phrase demonstrates that the FRR Capacity Rule 
should be read to only apply to New Large Load as it is defined at that time.  Accordingly, 
when IRAS is inactive, no new load will meet the definition of New Large Load.  In this 
circumstance, the FRR Capacity Rule would also effectively be inactive because there 
would be no identifiable New Large Load for the rule to apply to.   
Although it is possible to determine via the proposed PJM Tariff and RAA 
amendment language that the FRR Capacity Rule is effectively dormant at the same time 
that IRAS is dormant, the Commission should clarify that this is the case to avoid any 
confusion in the future.  Without clarification that the FRR Capacity Rule goes dormant 
simultaneous with IRAS, this aspect of the IRAS Proposal is unjust, unreasonable, and 
unduly discriminatory because it could be used to treat RPM load and FRR load differently 
 
28 See proposed definition of New Large Load; see proposed PJM Tariff, Attachment DD-4, section 
IV(b)(iii).

11 
without justification.  The FRR Capacity Rule, as described further below in section IV.B, 
is aimed at protecting the RPM market during periods of capacity scarcity in that market.  
PJM does not explain why the rule would continue to apply to FRR when capacity is not 
scarce.  Accordingly, PJM should clarify that AEP’s understanding of the rule is correct or 
the Commission should find the rule unjust and unreasonable and require PJM to modify 
it on compliance.   
B. 
PJM Should Clarify that When the Relevant In-Service Date for the 
Definition of New Large Load Resets, the Capacity Procurement 
Deadline under the FRR Capacity Rule Also Resets. 
The fixed date of June 1, 2027 in the FRR Capacity Rule is inconsistent with the 
flexible in-service date in the proposed definition of New Large Load.  PJM should clarify 
that when the in-service date for New Large Load resets, the procurement deadline for 
Existing Generation Capacity Resources under the FRR Capacity Rule likewise resets. 
PJM’s transmittal letter describes that the FRR Capacity Rule is proposed to ensure 
that “FRR Entities (or their New Large Loads) bring new capacity to the system to meet 
the New Large Loads’ resource adequacy needs, and precludes FRR Entities from 
satisfying load growth from New Large Loads with existing Capacity Resources that could 
potentially be lured from the RPM Auctions (and further exacerbating the shortage 
conditions in the capacity market).”29  Thus, the rationale for the FRR Capacity Rule 
appears to be to establish an obligation for FRR Entities that parallels the IRAS Proposal’s 
incentives for RPM load to bring its own new capacity.   
 
29 PJM Transmittal Letter at 73-74 (alteration in original).

12 
Under the FRR Capacity Rule as drafted, however, an FRR Entity cannot use 
Existing Generation Capacity Resources that were procured after June 1, 2027 to serve 
New Large Load even when IRAS goes dormant and then reactivates.  Thus, as written, 
the FRR Capacity Rule creates a likely scenario where in future years, if IRAS reactivates 
after a period of dormancy and the relevant in-service date for the definition of New Large 
Load has been reset, FRR Entities are still restricted from using Existing Generation 
Capacity Resources to satisfy New Large Load capacity requirements unless those Existing 
Generation Capacity Resources were procured prior to June 1, 2027.  This outcome is 
inconsistent with the intent of the IRAS rule and, if left unclarified, would put FRR Entities 
at a clear disadvantage to entities participating in the RPM.   
Accordingly, PJM should clarify that if the in-service date for New Large Load 
resets to June 1 of a future year, the cutoff date for procuring Existing Generation Capacity 
Resources under the FRR Capacity Rule also resets.  If the issue is not clarified, the IRAS 
Proposal will be unjust, unreasonable and unduly discriminatory with respect to the FRR 
Capacity Rule.  It will restrict FRR Entities to a greater extent than it would restrict RPM 
load.  Furthermore, such an inconsistent approach would thwart the aligned, parallel 
approach to FRR and RPM large load capacity that PJM describes in its transmittal letter 
as the justification for the novel restriction on the historic ability of FRR Entities to plan 
holistically for the capacity needs of their loads.

13 
C. 
PJM Should Clarify How FRR Entities Can Comply with Their 
Obligations Under the FRR Capacity Rule After IRAS is Reactivated. 
PJM should clarify that an FRR Entity can comply with the FRR Capacity Rule 
during years where IRAS is reactivated because the IRAS Proposal, as written, does not 
appear to provide sufficient notice for an FRR Entity to develop a compliant FRR Capacity 
Plan to provide for New Large Loads in reactivation years. 
Under the IRAS Proposal, if IRAS goes dormant, the determination of whether 
IRAS reactivates in a future delivery year is made pursuant to outcome of the final RPM 
auction for that delivery year, the Third Incremental Auction.30  This auction occurs only 
three to four months before the start of the delivery year.31  As described above in section 
IV.A, the mechanism for IRAS to go dormant and to reactivate is the definition of New 
Large Load and, because the FRR Capacity Rule hinges on its applicability to New Large 
Load, the FRR Capacity Rule should go dormant and reactivate at the same time as IRAS.32  
Thus, in a year where IRAS reactivates, the FRR Capacity Rule should also reactivate.   
However, as drafted, the FRR Capacity Rule appears to leave FRR Entities with 
only three to four months to ensure that their FRR Capacity Plan to serve New Large Load 
complies with the rule.  This timeline will be difficult, if not impossible, for FRR Entities 
to comply with because FRR Capacity Plans take years to develop.  FRR Entities must first 
submit their FRR Capacity Plan for a delivery year at least one month before the Base 
 
30 Proposed PJM Tariff, Attachment DD-4, section IV(b)(iii). 
31 PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., PJM Manual 18:  PJM Capacity Mkt., § 5.2, at 122 (rev. 62 Dec. 17, 2025), 
https://www.pjm.com/-/media/DotCom/documents/manuals/m18.ashx.  
32 As explained in section IV.A, FERC should clarify that this is the correct interpretation of the IRAS 
Proposal.

14 
Residual Auction for that delivery year, which occurs three years before the delivery year 
commences.33  The FRR Capacity Plan is then extended and updated annually.34  Compared 
to the usual multi-year timeline to develop an FRR Capacity Plan, three to four months is 
unrealistically short and would put FRR Entities at a severe disadvantage to RPM 
customers, who are able to comply with IRAS requirements on a shorter time frame.   
RPM load can comply with the IRAS Proposal requirements on a short time frame 
because they can comply either by (1) bringing their own new capacity or Reliability 
Backstop Procurement capacity, or by (2) being subject to IRAS reductions.  FRR load, 
however, can only comply with the IRAS proposal by providing sufficient capacity, 
because FRR load is not subject to IRAS.  FRR Entities are therefore disadvantaged by 
arbitrarily being placed in jeopardy of noncompliance as a result of the IRAS rules in 
reactivation years.  
Also, if the issue described in section IV.B above is not clarified and the FRR 
Capacity Rule restricts the use of Existing Generation Capacity Resources to only the 
resources procured before June 1, 2027, this will exacerbate the detrimental effects of the 
unreasonably short timeline for FRR Entities to develop a compliant FRR Capacity Plan, 
because they will be further restricted as to which capacity resources can be used to meet 
the capacity requirements of New Large Load.  
 
33 Proposed RAA, Schedule 8.1, section D.1; PJM Manual 18, § 5.2, at 121.  
34 Proposed RAA, Schedule 8.1, section D.1.

15 
To address these time constraints, PJM should clarify that upon reactivation, there 
is a one-year delay for the FRR Capacity Rule.  For example:  assume the IRAS is dormant 
entering 2035 for the prior delivery year but the Third Incremental Auction that occurs in 
February 2035 does not meet the conditions of Attachment DD-4, section IV(b)(iii) (i.e., 
does not clear sufficient capacity).  Under the IRAS Proposal, this would reactivate IRAS 
for the upcoming 2035/2036 delivery year and the definition of New Large Load would 
employ an in-service date of June 1, 2035.  Accordingly, under the IRAS Proposal, the 
FRR Capacity Rule would apply to New Large Load—that is, Large Load that goes into 
service after June 1, 2035.  Thus, under the FRR Capacity Rule, an FRR Entity would not 
be able to include in its FRR Capacity Plan any MW quantity of Existing Generation 
Capacity Resource in excess of what such FRR Entity owned or contracted by such FRR 
Entity prior to June 1, 2035, to serve New Large Load.35  This essentially gives the FRR 
Entity a short, three to four month period to contract with necessary supply to serve New 
Large Load.  This is simply not a reasonable amount of time to do so and puts FRR at a 
significant disadvantage to the rest of the PJM market.  Accordingly, in this example, FRR 
Entities should not have to comply with the FRR Capacity Rule until the start of the 
2036/2037 delivery year, and should have an additional year to procure the necessary 
Existing Generation Capacity Resources to serve New Large Load.  This will provide 
approximately sixteen months for FRR Entities to develop a compliant capacity plan for 
 
35 This statement assumes the requested clarification in section IV.B is accepted and the cutoff date becomes 
flexible, no longer fixed at June 1, 2027, but that the cutoff date is the same date as the IRAS reactivation 
date instead of providing a one-year delay as this section requests.

16 
New Large Load (which would still, in this example, be Large Load with an in-service date 
of June 1, 2035 or later).  The FRR Capacity Rule would restrict FRR Entities from using 
Existing Generation Capacity Resources that the FRR Entity procured after June 1, 2036, 
and would still provide the safeguards contemplated by the IRAS proposal at that time.  
Thus, upon reactivation, the FRR Capacity Rule would recognize that compliance with the 
rule reasonably requires more time than compliance with IRAS.  
1. 
This Issue Compounds if the FRR Capacity Rule Cutoff Date for 
Existing Generation Capacity Resources Remains Fixed at June 
1, 2027. 
If the issue described in section IV.B above is not clarified, and the FRR Capacity 
Rule restricts the use of Existing Generation Capacity Resources to only such resources 
procured before June 1, 2027—even far into the future after a period of IRAS dormancy—
then an FRR Entity may have already included Existing Generation Capacity Resources in 
their FRR Capacity Plan before it is determined that IRAS is reactivating for the upcoming 
delivery year.  During IRAS dormancy, an FRR Capacity Plan may be submitted prior to 
the Base Residual Auction (three years prior to the delivery year),36 and such a plan may 
utilize Existing Generation Capacity Resource that the FRR Entity procured after June 1, 
2027 to fulfill the capacity requirements of upcoming Large Load additions that will, if 
IRAS is reactivated after the Third Incremental Auction, be deemed New Large Load.37  In 
 
36 PJM Manual 18 § 5.2, at 121. 
37 This also raises a potential conflict with the Takings Clause of the Fifth Amendment, because FRR 
Entities would be restricted from utilizing their investment in the Existing Generation Capacity Resources 
they procured after June 1, 2027, with the reasonable expectation of using the procured capacity in their 
FRR Capacity Plan to serve upcoming large load additions.  The Takings Clause of the Fifth Amendment 
provides that “private property [shall not] be taken for public use, without just compensation.”  Regulatory 
takings occur where the government “imposes regulations that restrict an owner’s ability to use his own

17 
such a situation, the FRR Entity would be out of compliance with the FRR Capacity Rule 
as soon as IRAS (and the FRR Capacity Rule) is reactivated.  This is clearly not the intent 
of the IRAS proposal.  At a minimum, this issue should be addressed by clarifying the 
proposal is intended to operate as discussed in section IV.B and providing that FRR 
Capacity Rule’s cutoff date for procuring Existing Generation Capacity Resources resets 
along with the in-service date for New Large Load. 
2. 
If PJM does not clarify this issue, the IRAS Proposal is unjust 
and unreasonable. 
If PJM does not clarify that FRR Entities can comply with the FRR Capacity Rule 
in delivery years where IRAS reactivates after a dormant period, the IRAS Proposal is 
unjust, unreasonable and unduly discriminatory because it places FRR Entities at a 
significant disadvantage, as discussed above.   
V. 
CONCLUSION 
AEP respectfully requests that PJM clarify under its IRAS Proposal:  (1) that the 
FRR Capacity Rule will go dormant when IRAS goes dormant, (2) that the cutoff for 
procuring Existing Generation Capacity Resources under the FRR Capacity Rule will reset 
when the New Large Load in-service date resets, and (3) that FRR Entities can comply 
with the FRR Capacity Rule in years when the rule “reactivates” following a period of 
IRAS being dormant. 
 
property” but goes too far.  Cedar Point Nursery v. Hassid, 594 U.S. 139, 148 (2021).  A key consideration 
in evaluating whether a regulatory taking has occurred is the regulation’s interference with reasonable 
investment-backed expectations.  Penn Central Transportation Co. v. New York City, 438 U. S. 104, 124-
125 (1982).
